title: Sauptika: the night massacre
hook: a gigantic being blocks the gate of the sleeping camp, and every weapon Ashvatthama throws disappears into it
carry: he offers himself into the fire

segments.voice: Your line: two good arguments losing to one sleepless man. Yesterday Kripa gave good counsel under the banyan, lost the argument, and followed his nephew anyway. Whose advice did you go and ask? Day eight hundred fifty-two.

The Pandava camp is dark and quiet. Ashvatthama reaches the gate with Kripa and Kritavarma behind him. And the gate isn't empty. Something is standing there, so large it seems to fill the night. In Ganguli's English it's a being of enormous size, terrible to look at, blazing, wrapped in a tiger skin, with snakes for ornaments and many eyes. It doesn't speak. It just stands between Ashvatthama and the sleeping camp. Today, what happens at the gate, and the strange offering Ashvatthama makes before he can go through.
screen: `THE CAMP IS ASLEEP.` → `A BEING AT THE GATE.` → `IT DOESN'T SPEAK.`

segments.voice: Ashvatthama does what a warrior does. He attacks. He hurls weapon after weapon at the being, and the being swallows them. Every one vanishes into it, and it stands there untouched. Now he's empty-handed, at night, in front of something he can't fight. And now the text lets him think about the advice he ignored. In effect, he says: whoever turns away from the counsel of friends who wish him well comes to grief, and that's what I've done. Then he turns to Mahadeva, the great god, Shiva. He praises him with many names. And an altar of gold appears in front of him, with a fire blazing on it, and fierce companions of Shiva crowd around. Ashvatthama offers the only thing he has left. He offers himself. He steps into the fire. Shiva appears, and the text has him speak plainly. He has protected the Panchalas until now, out of regard for Krishna. But their time is over. Then Shiva gives Ashvatthama a sword and enters into his body, and Ashvatthama rises from the fire blazing with that power. It's a hard scene, and the epic doesn't smooth it over. The gate held until a man gave himself up completely. What came through the gate afterward was no longer just Ashvatthama's anger. Shiva's own words say the sleeping camp's time had come. Tomorrow, what that means.
screen: `THE WEAPONS VANISH` · `"I IGNORED MY FRIENDS"` · `HE OFFERS HIMSELF` · then, large: `SHIVA ENTERS HIM`

segments.voice: Sit still and picture a doorway you know well, your front door or a door at work. Breathe in, and imagine standing on its threshold, not yet through. Breathe out, and stay there, unhurried. Bring to mind a moment when you ran out of your usual tools and had to stop. What did you reach for then? Stay with that question for a few breaths without answering it. If you pray, you can rest in prayer with open hands. The bell holds the time.
Sauptika. The night book, where a being guards the gate, swallows every weapon, and opens only after a man offers himself into the fire.
Your line: he offers himself into the fire. Today, when your usual way of handling something stops working, notice what you reach for next. Day eight hundred fifty-two.

howItsDone: Hindus who worship Shiva as Mahadeva call on him by many names, and the hymn Ashvatthama offers at the gate is one of the places in the Mahabharata where those names are gathered.

fork.setup: you're Ashvatthama. every weapon you've thrown has vanished into the being at the gate. you're empty-handed. what do you do?
options: turn back and go find Kripa's elders.
turn to Mahadeva and offer yourself into the fire.
wait for the being to leave at dawn.
fork.reveal: he praises Mahadeva and offers himself; Shiva gives him a sword and enters his body.

original.note: Mahadeva, 'the great god': a name for Shiva, the god Ashvatthama turns to at the gate.

trapdoor: what you thought: Ashvatthama simply walked into the camp and attacked.
what it means: the gate was blocked until he offered himself to Shiva and Shiva entered him.
what a scholar hears: the epic frames the massacre as both a man's choice and a god's time, and leaves that tension for readers to hold.
